thread.title: Supreme Court Rules Men Can Be Victims of Sexual Violence, Upholds Woman's Conviction
thread.title_full: Supreme Court Rules Men Can Be Victims of Sexual Violence, Upholds Woman's Conviction

author: Headtopics
title: Supreme Court Rules Men Can Be Victims of Sexual Violence, Upholds Woman's Conviction
text: Supreme Court Rules Men Can Be Victims of Sexual Violence, Upholds Woman's Conviction The Supreme Court has ruled that men can also be victims of sexual violence, affirming the conviction of a woman for acts of lasciviousness against her 11-year-old nephew and stressing that laws must protect all victims regardless of gender. The Supreme Court has ruled that men can also be victims of sexual violence, underscoring that the law must protect all victims of abuse regardless of gender. In a 17-page en banc decision penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the high tribunal found a woman guilty of committing acts of lasciviousness against her 11-year-old nephew. The Court emphasized that while women have historically suffered sexual violence by men, the law must be adaptable to also recognize that men can be victims of perpetrators. It said that the context of rape must not be viewed only through the lens of gender, but more importantly, of power.Rape Defined As Issue Of Power ImbalanceAt its core, rape is an issue of power, an imposition of someone's dominance to violate the bodily autonomy of another, the SC said. This power imbalance can manifest in many ways such as through differences in gender, age, socioeconomic stature, professional authority, or education. In rape, the perpetrator uses this power imbalance to coerce or manipulate the victim into submitting to their will or to make it impossible for the victim to refuse their advances, it added.The Court also pointed out that many countries have now adopted gender-neutral rape laws to protect everyone's sexual autonomy from the harm of non-consensual penetrative sexual acts. Court records indicated that the child, who visited his father's relatives, was asleep when the woman woke him up, ordered him to remove his clothes, and made him lie on her bed. She then engaged in sexual intercourse with him.The child did not protest at first because he felt curious about what would happen, but after the incident, he felt ashamed and considered ending his life. The child was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from the sexual abuse as indicated by a psychological debriefing and supportive psychotherapy, the high tribunal said. The woman argued that the child consented to the sexual act but the high court disagreed.Legal Age Of Consent Raises Legal QuestionsIt explained that at the time of the incident in 2018, the age of sexual consent was 12 years old. Because the child was only 11, he was deemed legally incapable of giving consent. This has since been increased to under 16 years old following the enactment of RA 11648 in 2022. Leonen in the same ruling clarified, however, that the proper offense was statutory acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code, not RA 7610.Citing jurisprudence, the Court explained that RA 7610 applies when a minor appears to consent to sexual activity due to the coercion or influence of an adult. It does not apply when a minor is entirely unaware, unconscious, or unable to give legal consent, as in this case.The woman was charged with statutory acts of lasciviousness because, at the time of the offense, her acts did not fall within the legal definition of rape under Article 266-A of the RPC. The law then limited the act of rape to a man inserting his penis into a woman's vagina, as well as the insertion of a penis or any object into another person's genital, it stressed.However, the high tribunal said RA 11648, enacted in 2022, expanded the definition of rape, now stating that it may be committed by any person who has carnal knowledge of another person under the circumstances specified by law. The use of the term person in the law instead of specifying the perpetrator's gender allows for the commission of rape even by women, the high court said.Court Examines Patriarchal Roots Of Rape LawsDespite this amendment, the Court noted that some rulings continue to describe rape as a crime committed by men against women. It traced this view to older, patriarchal rape laws that were originally designed not to protect women from violence, but to punish men for taking women, who were considered the property of their fathers or husbands, through rape. These beliefs about rape are not only sexist, but also exclude male victims who suffer the same trauma.The failure to recognize that they can be victims of rape can also make it harder for them to realize that they were violated, Leonen said. Thus, while there must be recognition of the historical injustice women have suffered, the law, as well as its interpretation, must be resilient enough to provide equal protection to all victims and guard against stereotypes that all women are victims and all men are perpetrators.When laws are not gender-neutral, male victims suffer twice: once at the hands of their abuser and second through the judicial system, he added. The Court reiterated that the sexual violence suffered by the child caused him intense shame and guilt and left him traumatized. The woman also made him believe that he had agreed to and enjoyed what was done to him. If the genders had been reversed, the incident would have been considered rape.However, as it stands, the acts penalized do not fall within the legal definition of rape as provided by law at the time of the crime, it explained. The woman was found guilty of statutory acts of lasciviousness under Article 336 of the Revised Penal Code. She was sentenced to prison for nine to 16 years and ordered to pay P250,000 in civil indemnity and damages.
summary: In a 17-page en banc decision penned by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the high tribunal found a woman guilty of committing acts of lasciviousness against her 11-year-old nephew. Court records indicated that the child, who visited his father's relatives, was asleep when the woman woke him up, ordered him to remove his clothes, and made him lie on her bed. The child was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from the sexual abuse as indicated by a psychological debriefing and supportive psychotherapy, the high tribunal said.
